name: pgpdump
why: Dumps the packet structure of PGP messages, a good way to see how OpenPGP data is actually laid out.

brief.what_it_is: pgpdump is a command-line PGP packet visualizer written by Kazu Yamamoto. You give it a PGP file, either binary or ASCII-armored, and it prints the packet structure: each packet's tag, length, and version, plus its fields such as signature type, hash and public-key algorithms, creation times, salts, fingerprints, and signature bytes. It covers OpenPGP (RFC 9580 and RFC 4880), the post-quantum algorithms of RFC 9980, PGP version 2 (RFC 1991), and the LibrePGP extensions generated by GnuPG. The homepage's example takes the RFC 9580 Appendix A.7 signed message and prints each packet with its fields.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it is very hard to understand the data structure inside a PGP file by looking at it, so pgpdump shows the packet layout in readable form.
brief.how_it_works: PGP output is binary or ASCII armor (Base64-like text between BEGIN and END lines). pgpdump decodes the armor, walks the packet sequence, and prints a labelled line for each packet and each field. The homepage shows this with a sample where the one-pass signature, literal data, and signature packets are listed in order with their algorithms and byte counts.

commands_seen.context: Shows the ASCII-armored sample file (the RFC 9580 Appendix A.7 signed message) before it is dumped.
Dumps the packet structure of sig.pgp, printing each packet's tag, size, and fields such as signature type, hash algorithm, public-key algorithm, and times.

brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no install steps beyond a source download link and a note that a Git repository is on GitHub. Nothing about hardware, accounts, or runtimes was seen. The brew formula name is pgpdump, and the executable is pgpdump.
brief.standout: It is a reference-grade dumper that tracks the newest specs, including post-quantum OpenPGP from RFC 9980 and the GnuPG LibrePGP extensions, and it has been around since December 1998. It is a practical way to learn the OpenPGP wire format from real data.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the homepage shows: it lists version 0.38 dated 25 Sep 2026 and says a Git repository is on GitHub. I did not check the repository's commit history or release page, so the exact date of the last commit is unknown.
brief.caveats: The homepage does not give a licence, supported platforms, or build requirements. It is a dumper only, so it does not verify signatures or decrypt messages. The sample output is shown in the page, but I did not run the tool.

entry.title: pgpdump
entry.tldr: Prints the packet structure inside a PGP file, so you can see how OpenPGP messages, signatures and keys are actually laid out.
entry.deeper_look:
pgpdump reads a PGP file, either binary or ASCII-armored, and prints one labelled entry per packet. Each entry shows the tag, length and version, then its fields: signature type, hash and public-key algorithms, creation times, salts, fingerprints and signature bytes.

The homepage explains why it exists: "It's very hard to understand the data structure inside this." A PGP message is Base64-like text between BEGIN and END lines, and decoding that by eye gets you nowhere. pgpdump decodes the armor, walks the packet sequence and prints it in readable form. The homepage example is a signed message from RFC 9580 Appendix A.7, which lists a one-pass signature packet, a literal data packet and a signature packet in order.

The idea underneath is that OpenPGP is a stream of tagged, length-prefixed packets. Once you can see them, keys, signatures and encrypted messages stop being opaque blobs. You can read the spec on one side and real data on the other. It covers OpenPGP (RFC 9580 and RFC 4880), the post-quantum algorithms of RFC 9980, the older PGP version 2 (RFC 1991) and the LibrePGP extensions generated by GnuPG. The first release was in December 1998.

entry.whats_unique: It has tracked OpenPGP since 1998 and still follows the newest specs, including post-quantum OpenPGP and the GnuPG LibrePGP extensions. It is a practical way to learn the wire format from real data.
entry.caveats: It only dumps packets: it does not verify signatures or decrypt anything, and the homepage lists no platform or build details.
